title: Creative New York
plain_title: The state of the city's arts and creative economy
what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, examining the size and health of the city's arts and creative economy and setting out ten proposals for city and state policymakers.
background: The creative sector accounts for more than 7 percent of private sector employment in the five boroughs and spans ten core industries, from performing arts and film to advertising, design and architecture.

findings.plain: The creative sector remains one of the city's largest employers, with a workforce of more than 326,000 in 2024.
findings.quote: arts and creative industries employ more than 326,000 New Yorkers

findings.plain: The number of working artists has dropped since the pandemic began, with especially steep declines among dancers and actors.
findings.quote: the city has seen an 18.8 percent decline in dancers, an 8 percent

findings.plain: Film and television employment grew steeply before 2020 and has fallen since, a reversal seen in advertising, architecture and design as well.
findings.quote: film and TV jobs in New York City are down by 19.1 percent

findings.plain: The city is losing share of the national creative workforce.
findings.quote: creative economy has declined from 9.3 percent to 8.6 percent since 2019.

findings.plain: Cultural venues have closed in significant numbers since 2020, with operators citing changed audience habits and rising insurance costs.
findings.quote: Nearly 50 theaters, music clubs, museums, and galleries have shuttered since 2020

findings.plain: Creative workers earn well below the national average once the cost of living is counted, and the gap has widened over a decade.
findings.quote: about 23 percent less than the national average after adjusting for the city’s high cost of living

findings.plain: The report also documents growth, including new venues and a sharp rise in cultural nonprofits outside Manhattan.
findings.quote: nonprofits have grown 73.8 percent in Queens

recommendations: Tackle the affordability crisis with a large increase in housing production, building on the City of Yes zoning reforms with more as-of-right zoning near transit, an end to remaining parking minimums, faster permitting and review, broader legalization of accessory dwellings and stronger preservation tools.

Create 5,000 artist-preference housing units by 2030, with clear guidance from the Department of Housing Preservation and Development, a biennial artist survey, a citywide artist live/work standard, artist set-asides in office-to-residential conversions and an artist housing accelerator.
Launch the city's first five-borough cultural festival, coordinated by the city and using streets, plazas, parks and city-owned properties, with streamlined permitting for outdoor programming.
Launch a portable benefits pilot for freelancers and self-employed artists, administered by a nonprofit partner and funded proportionally by employers, platforms and public dollars.
Establish a city-facilitated pooled insurance program that lets cultural organizations and small venues buy coverage together at lower rates, with subsidies for the smallest organizations.

Create a Cultural Ownership Fund to help mission-driven groups keep or acquire space, expand shared back-office services and shared spaces, and reform the Temporary Place of Assembly permitting process.

Expand the Economic Development Corporation's creative industries work into a core pillar of its strategy, dedicate at least 1 percent of capital budgets to public art or creative placemaking, and expand shared production hubs and signature industry events.
Expand the Public Artists in Residence program tenfold and create full-time civic artist positions in agencies that have never hosted one, each with its own art initiative.

Create dedicated recurring revenue for the arts, such as a voluntary hotel stay surcharge feeding a parks and culture fund and pilot cultural districts, and make Cultural Development Fund payments timelier with a new tier of grantees for midsized organizations.

Launch a Creative Pathways and Talent Pipeline Initiative spanning public schools and CUNY, including a creative economy focus in FutureReadyNYC, sequential arts learning in every grade band, and paid internships and mentorship for CUNY students.
